paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, planners regarded dense cities with suspicion. Overcrowded tenements were associated with disease and poverty, and the preferred model was the suburb: detached houses, gardens, cars. Today, many urbanists argue the opposite, that density is essential to sustainable and prosperous cities. I find this case largely persuasive, though not without qualification.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The environmental argument is the most straightforward. Residents of compact cities typically travel shorter distances and use public transport more, so their per capita emissions are lower. A flat shares walls with its neighbours and therefore needs less energy for heating than a detached house. A study comparing American cities found that households in the densest neighbourhoods produced roughly half the transport emissions of those in the sprawling suburbs.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There are economic benefits too. Concentrating people and businesses makes it easier to share ideas, find specialised workers and support services such as hospitals and theatres. Economists use the term agglomeration to describe this effect, and it helps to explain why productivity is higher in large cities. At the same time, density reduces the cost of infrastructure per resident, since each kilometre of road or pipe serves more people.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Yet density has real costs, which advocates sometimes understate. Residents of crowded areas report more noise and less privacy. Rising demand can push up housing prices, displacing existing communities, as has happened in San Francisco and parts of London. And dense does not necessarily mean pleasant. Poorly designed high-rise estates have in the past isolated residents rather than connected them. The success of density depends on design: green space, mixed uses and good public transport are not luxuries but conditions.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A balanced position would therefore encourage density in places well served by transport, while insisting on high standards of design and on genuinely affordable housing. Cities that grow upward without these safeguards risk replacing the problems of sprawl with those of inequality. Cities that grow outward, however, will almost certainly struggle to meet climate targets. The choice is not between density and its absence but between well-planned and badly planned growth.
